title: What Actually Drives the Growth of Cities
text:
For most of human history the overwhelming majority of people lived in the countryside and worked the land. That has changed within a few generations. More than half the world's population now lives in towns and cities, and the share is still climbing. I want to look at what actually produces that shift, because it is not one process but three.

The first is rural-to-urban migration. People move because cities concentrate wages, schooling and services, and because mechanised agriculture needs fewer hands than it once did, so a push and a pull operate together. The second is natural increase. Cities grow from within, since migrants are typically young adults of childbearing age, and before long births in the city outnumber arrivals to it. The third is reclassification, which involves nobody moving at all: a village that expands past a statistical threshold is simply counted as a town. The consequence sociologists emphasise is that growth has outrun formal housing and infrastructure in much of the world. Large populations live in self-built settlements with insecure tenure. Researchers consistently find dense networks of mutual support inside them, so these are not disorganised places; but their residents carry the cost of services the formal city was never extended to provide.
points: Most people now live in towns and cities, a reversal of most of human history.
Rural-to-urban migration is driven by urban wages and services and by agriculture needing fewer workers.
Cities also grow by natural increase, because migrants are mostly young adults and births soon outnumber arrivals.
Some urban growth is reclassification: a village passing a threshold is counted as a town without anyone moving.
Growth has outpaced formal housing, so many people live in self-built settlements with insecure tenure.
These settlements have strong mutual support networks but lack services the formal city never extended to them.
